lessonTitle: Water-soluble and Fat-soluble Vitamins: Coenzymes and Deficiency Syndromes

blocks.text: On long sea voyages in the eighteenth century, sailors who ate only salted meat and biscuit grew weak, their gums bled and swelled, and old scars that had healed years earlier broke open again. Citrus fruit cured them within days. The missing substance was vitamin C, which the body needs to build stable collagen. Vitamins are small organic molecules we cannot make in sufficient amounts, and most act as coenzymes, so deficiency stops specific reactions.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** Vitamins are divided by solubility. **Water-soluble vitamins** (the B group and vitamin C) are mostly excreted in urine, are stored little (vitamin B12 is the notable exception, stored in liver for years) and are largely used as **coenzymes**. **Fat-soluble vitamins** (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles, stored in liver and fat, can accumulate to toxic levels, and have more varied roles (hormone-like, antioxidant, gene regulation, carboxylation). Fat malabsorption (cholestasis, coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency) therefore risks deficiency of A, D, E and K.

blocks.title: Coenzyme
blocks.text: A coenzyme is a small organic cofactor (often derived from a vitamin) that binds an enzyme and carries chemical groups, electrons or hydrogen atoms during a reaction. Without the vitamin, the enzyme cannot function, and the reactions it supports back up.

rows: Pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase, transketolase
Redox reactions, e.g. succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase)
Dermatitis, hair loss; raw egg white (avidin)
One-carbon transfer for purine and thymidylate synthesis
Megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects in pregnancy
Megaloblastic anaemia, neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration)
blocks.caption: B vitamins, their active coenzymes and the clinical consequences of deficiency.

blocks.markdown: **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** is a reducing agent and a cofactor for **prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases**, which hydroxylate proline and lysine residues in procollagen so that the triple helix can be stabilised by hydrogen bonds and cross-linked. It keeps the iron of these enzymes in the ferrous form and also enhances non-haem iron absorption. Deficiency causes **scurvy**: weak collagen leads to bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, bruising, poor wound healing and loosened teeth.

blocks.title: Reasoning from a deficient enzyme to its vitamin
blocks.prompt: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use has a high blood lactate and pyruvate and a low red-cell transketolase activity that rises when thiamine pyrophosphate is added in vitro. Which vitamin is deficient, and why do pyruvate and lactate accumulate?

steps.text: A rise in enzyme activity after adding TPP in vitro shows the enzyme was short of that coenzyme.
TPP is derived from thiamine (vitamin B1), so thiamine is deficient.
TPP is needed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. With reduced activity, pyruvate cannot enter the citric acid cycle and is reduced to lactate.
Neurons depend on aerobic glucose oxidation, so ATP falls and neurological disease (Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, eye-movement abnormalities) follows.

blocks.answer: Thiamine deficiency. Because glucose metabolism increases thiamine demand, thiamine is given before or with glucose in at-risk patients (a clinical teaching point, not individual advice).

blocks.markdown: **Niacin and units.** Niacin can also be made from the amino acid tryptophan, so intake is expressed as **niacin equivalents (NE)**: 1 mg NE = 1 mg preformed niacin or 60 mg dietary tryptophan. Deficiency (pellagra) is seen where maize is the staple (its niacin is bound) and the diet is low in tryptophan. In carcinoid syndrome and Hartnup disease tryptophan is diverted or poorly absorbed, which may also cause pellagra.

blocks.title: Niacin equivalents
blocks.prompt: A diet provides 10 mg of preformed niacin and 300 mg of tryptophan per day. Calculate the niacin equivalents.

rows: 11-cis-retinal in rhodopsin for vision; retinoic acid regulates gene transcription and epithelial differentiation
Night blindness, xerophthalmia, keratomalacia, infection risk
Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxy): raises calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation
Haemolytic anaemia in premature infants; neuropathy and ataxia
Cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate in clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
blocks.caption: The fat-soluble vitamins.

blocks.markdown: **Vitamin D in detail.** Skin 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted by UVB light to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3); diet supplies vitamin D2 or D3. The liver adds a hydroxyl group at carbon 25 (**25-hydroxylase**), giving calcifediol (the usual storage and measurement form), and the kidney adds the 1-alpha hydroxyl group (**1-alpha-hydroxylase**, stimulated by PTH and low phosphate) to give active **calcitriol**. Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate. In deficiency, osteoid is laid down but not mineralised: in children this causes **rickets** (bowed legs, widened wrist and costochondral junctions, delayed growth) with low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised PTH; adults develop **osteomalacia** with bone pain and proximal weakness. Vitamin D is measured in micrograms or international units, where **1 microgram equals 40 IU**.

blocks.title: Converting vitamin D units
blocks.prompt: An infant supplement provides 10 micrograms of cholecalciferol. How many international units is this?

steps.text: 10 micrograms x 40 IU per microgram = 400 IU.

blocks.answer: 400 IU. (Quoted as a unit conversion example; supplementation decisions are individual.)

blocks.title: Vitamin K and the clotting factors
blocks.text: Gamma-carboxylation converts glutamate residues of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X to gamma-carboxyglutamate, which binds calcium and lets the factors attach to phospholipid surfaces. The reaction uses reduced vitamin K and regenerates it by vitamin K epoxide reductase, which warfarin inhibits. Newborns have low stores and a sterile gut, which is why vitamin K deficiency bleeding is prevented by prophylaxis at birth.

blocks.title: Match the vitamin to the verb
blocks.text: Thiamine decarboxylates, riboflavin and niacin shuttle electrons, pantothenate carries acyl groups, biotin carboxylates, pyridoxal phosphate transaminates, folate carries one-carbon units, B12 rearranges and methylates, vitamin C hydroxylates collagen, vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors.

points: B vitamins are converted to coenzymes (TPP, FAD, NAD+, CoA, PLP, biotin, THF, cobalamin forms) that support specific reactions; deficiency produces predictable syndromes such as beriberi, pellagra and megaloblastic anaemia.
Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen synthesis, so deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin A supports vision and epithelia, D (as calcitriol) supports calcium and bone, E is a membrane antioxidant, and K carboxylates clotting factors.
Fat-soluble vitamins need fat absorption and can accumulate to toxic levels.

questions.stem: Which vitamin and coenzyme pairing is correct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: niacin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+.
distractorRationale.b: Riboflavin gives FAD and FMN, not NAD+.
distractorRationale.c: Thiamine gives thiamine pyrophosphate, not FAD.
distractorRationale.d: Pyridoxine gives pyridoxal phosphate; coenzyme A is derived from pantothenic acid.

questions.explanation: Niacin is converted to NAD+ and NADP+, the coenzymes of many dehydrogenases. The other pairs mismatch the vitamin and coenzyme: riboflavin makes FAD, thiamine makes TPP and pyridoxine makes PLP.

questions.stem: A man on a fad diet eats large quantities of raw egg whites for several weeks and develops dermatitis and hair thinning. Which enzyme reaction is most directly impaired?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin, the cofactor of pyruvate carboxylase and other carboxylases.
distractorRationale.b: Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires thiamine, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD+, not biotin.
distractorRationale.d: Dihydrofolate reduction requires NADPH and DHFR; it does not involve biotin.

questions.explanation: Avidin in raw egg white binds biotin tightly and prevents its absorption, so biotin-dependent carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase fail. Dermatitis and hair loss are classic features of biotin deficiency.

questions.stem: A 6-day-old breast-fed newborn who did not receive vitamin K at birth has melaena and bruising. Which biochemical defect explains the bleeding?

options.text: Failure of gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX and X
Failure of hydroxylation of proline in collagen
Failure of calcium absorption in the gut

questions.correctOptionText: Failure of gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX and X

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation, which lets these factors bind calcium and phospholipid.
distractorRationale.b: Hydroxylation of proline needs vitamin C and affects collagen, not clotting factor activation.
distractorRationale.c: Rhodopsin regeneration needs vitamin A and affects vision.
distractorRationale.d: Poor calcium absorption results from vitamin D deficiency and does not cause this bleeding syndrome.

questions.explanation: Without vitamin K, clotting factors II, VII, IX and X are made but remain uncarboxylated and cannot bind calcium, so coagulation fails. Newborns have low stores and little vitamin K-producing gut flora, which is why prophylaxis is given at birth.

questions.stem: A child with severe fat malabsorption develops difficulty seeing in dim light and dry, roughened corneas. Which vitamin deficiency is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore of rhodopsin, and deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia.
distractorRationale.b: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding and poor healing.
distractorRationale.c: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neurological damage.

questions.explanation: Vitamin A, a fat-soluble vitamin, is needed for the visual pigment rhodopsin and for epithelial integrity. Fat malabsorption lowers its absorption, producing night blindness and corneal drying (xerophthalmia).

questions.stem: A malnourished man with chronic alcohol use is admitted with confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Why might giving a large glucose infusion alone worsen his encephalopathy?

options.text: Glucose oxidation increases demand for thiamine pyrophosphate in pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, depleting an already low supply
Glucose inhibits intestinal absorption of vitamin B12
Glucose is converted to ethanol in the brain
Glucose blocks the action of vitamin K

questions.correctOptionText: Glucose oxidation increases demand for thiamine pyrophosphate in pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, depleting an already low supply

distractorRationale.a: Correct: thiamine-dependent enzymes are needed to burn glucose, so a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a thiamine-deficient patient.
distractorRationale.b: Glucose does not block B12 absorption.
distractorRationale.c: Human brain does not convert glucose to ethanol.
distractorRationale.d: Glucose does not antagonise vitamin K.

questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase need thiamine pyrophosphate, and glucose metabolism increases the demand for them. In a thiamine-deficient patient the extra glucose can unmask or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy, which is why thiamine is given before or with glucose in at-risk patients (a teaching point rather than individual advice).

questions.stem: True or false: vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen.
questions.explanation: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate to keep their iron in the ferrous state. Without it collagen is poorly hydroxylated and unstable, producing the bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and poor wound healing of scurvy.

questions.stem: A vitamin D supplement label states that each capsule contains 25 micrograms of cholecalciferol. Given that 1 microgram equals 40 international units, how many international units does one capsule contain?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the mass by the conversion factor gives 25 x 40 = 1000 IU. Knowing this conversion is useful because laboratories, guidelines and labels use either micrograms or international units.

questions.stem: A diet supplies 8 mg of preformed niacin and 480 mg of tryptophan per day. Taking 60 mg of tryptophan as equivalent to 1 mg of niacin, calculate the niacin equivalents in mg per day.
questions.explanation: Tryptophan contributes 480 / 60 = 8 mg niacin equivalents. Adding the preformed niacin gives 8 + 8 = 16 mg, showing how tryptophan can partially protect against pellagra.

questions.stem: Match six of the B vitamins to their active coenzyme forms, and for each give one reaction or reaction type that it supports.
markingGuide: Thiamine to thiamine pyrophosphate: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase or transketolase
Riboflavin to FAD or FMN: redox reactions such as succinate dehydrogenase
Niacin to NAD+ or NADP+: hydride transfer in dehydrogenases
Pantothenic acid to coenzyme A: acyl group transfer
Pyridoxine to pyridoxal phosphate: transamination or decarboxylation
Biotin: carboxylation reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase
Folate to tetrahydrofolate: one-carbon transfer; B12 to methylcobalamin or adenosylcobalamin: methionine synthase or methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (any six pairs with a reaction each)
questions.explanation: Each B vitamin is converted to a coenzyme that supports a characteristic type of reaction. Remembering the reaction type for each coenzyme predicts which pathway fails when the vitamin is deficient.

questions.stem: Describe how vitamin D is synthesised and activated, state its actions, and relate its deficiency to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
markingGuide: 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin converted by UVB to cholecalciferol; also supplied by diet
Liver 25-hydroxylation gives calcifediol (storage and measurement form)
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylation (stimulated by PTH and low phosphate) gives active calcitriol
Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate and supports bone mineralisation
Deficiency: osteoid formed but not mineralised
Rickets in children: bowed legs, widened wrists and costochondral junctions, growth failure, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and PTH
Osteomalacia in adults: bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fractures
questions.explanation: Vitamin D acts as a hormone precursor that is activated in two steps in the liver and kidney, and its main action is to supply calcium and phosphate for mineralisation. When it is lacking, unmineralised osteoid accumulates, causing rickets in the growing skeleton and osteomalacia in the mature one.
